newsitem.title: UK: Funds hit high-profile LME metals, sentiment edgy.
newsitem.headline: Funds hit high-profile LME metals, sentiment edgy.

text.p: Investment fund selling and distressed liquidation hit several high-profile metal contracts on the London Metal Exchange (LME) on Tuesday as market sentiment soured, traders said.
Copper was the main casualty, diving to the lowest levels since December 1996 as it resumed a downturn that started last week.
But aluminium and zinc were also mauled by the speculators, with the current tightness in both markets counting for little.
"These markets are oversold...but nobody wants to buy at the moment because they think they can pick it up cheaper," one trader said.
Copper prices at one stage were trading at $2,118 a tonne, showing a loss of nearly eight percent from levels that prevailed only last Thursday.

Traders said crucial chart support at $2,120 held once the sell-stops (pre-set sale orders) had run their course and the market struggled back to the mid-$2,140s. But the market's prospects did not look positive.
Metal inventories were rising remorselessly as summer shutdowns at end-users bit into demand. Because of that, the market's long-running backwardation or spot premium had been erased.
Forward months were still in backwardation, but these were sagging as metal was made available for these dates, traders said.
Aluminium lost $20 under fund selling as investment interests who bought metal when prices were rising from $1,600 a few weeks ago opted to take profits.
"Another factor is what is happening on the Dow recently," a trader said.
Nearby tightness, which flared up wickedly on Tuesday, was not enough to stem the decline as the backwardations were not seen being sustained.
Earlier on Tuesday, there was a premium to borrow "tommorrow/next day" aluminium (belated business against the previous day's cash) of $21 a tonne.
LME authorities were monitoring the action, but did not intervene. By late afternoon prices were skirting near lows of $1,633.
Traders said that the tightness would eventually be defused by metal being delivered into warehouses in coming weeks.

Zinc similarly tumbled, although traders voiced caution as there might be a sting in the tail in September when Chinese short positions matured. Zinc bounced off a $1,461 low to settle near $1,475, but remained easier.
